# Sharp cap/section hinge bounds, integer regression, and an attained-stress obstruction

This note supplies a local moment identity for the normal full-cover stress in `candidate 2d0fea5cdbf7c841`. It does not establish an OC budget. In particular, the attained minimizer in Section 4 has budget strictly above one half, not below the OC constant.

## 1. The sharp individual-fiber inequality

Let `K subset R^d` be a convex body, `d>=1`, let `u` be a unit vector, and set `L(x)=u.x-b`. Define
\[
 c=|K\cap\{L\ge0\}|,\quad
 h=\int_K L_+\,dx,\quad
 S=\mathcal H_{d-1}(K\cap\{L=0\}).
\]
For a proper cut, `c,S>0`, and
\[
 \boxed{\quad h\le\frac d{d+1}\frac{c^2}{S}.\quad}
\tag{1}
\]
Equivalently, if `g_+` and `g_0` are the ordinary cap and section centroids,
\[
 u\cdot(g_+-g_0)=\frac hc
 \le\frac d{d+1}\frac cS.
\tag{2}
\]
Thus (2) compares a directional distance of two centroids with their *actual different-dimensional measures*; it does not identify their laws.

For completeness, put `F(t)=|K intersect {L>=t}|`. Brunn–Minkowski applied to the cap sets makes `F^(1/d)` concave on its positive interval. At a proper section, the coarea identity and interior continuity of the section area give `F'(0)=-S`. Its tangent therefore gives
\[
 F(t)\le c(1-St/(dc))^d\qquad(t\ge0)
\]
where the positive support cannot extend beyond `dc/S`. Integrating the survival function proves (1). This also works in dimension one, where the section has counting measure one and the identity is `h=c^2/2`.

Equality holds when the positive cap is a cone with base its section and an apex on the positive side: if its height is H, then `c=SH/d` and `h=SH^2/[d(d+1)]`. Simplicial cones give equality within polytopes in every dimension.

At a supporting facet, (1) remains true for any effective coarea section density between zero and one. At a full lower-facet cap it follows by the limiting full-facet inequality, because reducing S weakens its upper bound. At an empty upper-facet cap both c and h are zero. These are precisely the effective boundary sections allowed by the stress theorem. A positive cap with effective S=0 must be retained separately; division by its section measure is not legitimate.

The corresponding sharp *full-fiber* centroid inequality
\[
 S(u\cdot g_K-b)
 \le dc\left[1-\frac d{d+1}\left(\frac{|K|}{c}\right)^{1/d}\right]
\]
is already proved in `candidate 06cc7d27835f78bc`. It is not a new conclusion of this note.

## 2. Exact aggregation requires a slope variance

Now take finitely many mixed fibers and one ambient cap with unit continuous normal u. For each fiber use its affine restriction to define `c_z,h_z,S_z` as above, with one consistent effective section density. Put
\[
 I=\{z:S_z>0\},\quad C=\sum_{z\in I}c_z,\quad
 S=\sum_{z\in I}S_z,\quad
 h_*=\sum_{z\notin I}h_z.
\]
Assume `S>0`. Let `delta_z=c_z/S_z` for `z in I`. Summing (1) and expanding a square gives the sharp bound
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \sum_z h_z\le h_*+\frac d{d+1}
 \left[\frac{C^2}{S}
       +\sum_{z\in I}S_z\left(\delta_z-\frac CS\right)^2\right].
 \quad}
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed the bracket is exactly `sum_I c_z^2/S_z`. The extra term is nonnegative and cannot be dropped by Cauchy–Schwarz: that inequality goes in the opposite direction. Equality holds whenever all the positive cap fibers are cones attaining (1); when `d=1`, equality is automatic for proper interval cuts.

The zero-section contribution `h_*` is explicit. In particular (3) makes no unsupported claim about fully included fibers whose effective sections vanish.

## 3. What the integer first moments detect, and what they miss

Suppose every positive cap mass has positive section measure, so `h_*=0` and C is the entire cap mass. Put a probability law on the section indices by `pi_z=S_z/S`, and let
\[
 \bar z_s=E_\pi Z,\qquad
 \bar z_c=C^{-1}\sum_z zc_z,\qquad
 \Sigma=E_\pi[(Z-\bar z_s)(Z-\bar z_s)^T].
\]
Then
\[
 v:=E_\pi[(Z-\bar z_s)(\delta-C/S)]
    =\frac CS(\bar z_c-\bar z_s).
\tag{4}
\]
This vector lies in the range of the positive semidefinite matrix Sigma: every vector in its kernel has constant pairing with Z on the section support and hence zero pairing with v. Let `beta=Sigma^+ v`, where `Sigma^+` is its Moore–Penrose inverse on its range. Orthogonal projection in the finite weighted Euclidean space gives the exact identity
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_\pi(\delta)
 =v^T\Sigma^+v+
 E_\pi[\delta-C/S-\beta\cdot(Z-\bar z_s)]^2.
\tag{5}
\]
It follows simply by expanding the square, using `Sigma beta=v`. Thus the base first moments detect the affine-in-base component of the slope variation, while a nonnegative orthogonal residual remains.

For a normal stress with cap multiplier r and contact measure of mass `C+rS`, the base equations give
\[
 \bar z_{\rm contact}
 =\frac{C\bar z_c+rS\bar z_s}{C+rS},
\]
so they specify the vector in (4). Even the stronger equality
`bar z_contact=bar z_c=bar z_s` only sets v to zero. It does not set the last term in (5) to zero. If one separately knows that `delta_z` is affine in z on the section support, then (5) does imply zero variance under this equality; that additional geometric condition is not automatic.

## 4. An exact global normal hinge minimum with positive residual variance

Take `n=d=1` and
\[
 C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(
 \{-1\}\times[-1/2,1/2],\
 \{0\}\times[-1,1],\
 \{1\}\times[-1/2,1/2]\bigr).
\]
Its actual three integer fibers are exactly the displayed intervals: their widths `(1,2,1)` are concave and their centers are zero. The total mixed mass is `M=4`. Fix two caps and any budget `tau in (1/2,1)`.

Consider the full cover
\[
 L_+(z,x)=x,\qquad L_-(z,x)=-x.
\]
Each cap has mass C=2, hinge `Psi_+=Psi_-=3/4`, and actual section mass S=3. Both section centroids and both cap integer-base means are zero.

This cover is a **global hinge minimizer** under this normalization and budget. The following pointwise fiber argument proves the claim against every other two-cap cover with continuous normals of absolute value one, including arbitrary integer tilts. In one interval of length w, two halfline caps with the same orientation can cover the interval only if one cap contains it entirely. That one hinge is at least `w^2/2`. If the orientations are opposite, write their thresholds as p for `x>=p` and q for `x<=q`. If `p<=q`, their two hinges pointwise dominate `|x-(p+q)/2|`, whose integral over the interval is at least `w^2/4`. If `p>q`, full coverage forces the open gap `(q,p)` to miss the interval interior; one cap then contains the whole interval, again costing at least `w^2/2`. Thus every two-cap cover costs at least `w^2/4` in every fiber. Summation gives the lower bound
\[
 \frac14(1^2+2^2+1^2)=\frac32,
\]
attained by the displayed midpoint split. Its cap masses are strictly below `tau M`, so it is feasible at every stated interior budget.

Here is the exact normal stress. For each fiber z choose its actual interior contact `(z,0)`, assign the two cap weights `p_z+=p_z-=1/2`, and choose coverage multipliers
\[
 (\eta_{-1},\eta_0,\eta_1)=(1,2,1).
\]
Take cap-budget multipliers `r_+=r_-=0`, consistent full section densities one, and objective multiplier one. The contact weights balance the continuous normals. The cap masses are `sum eta_z/2=2`; cap and contact integer first moments are zero. Their continuous contact and section moments are zero, while the cap moments are `X_+=3/4` and `X_-=-3/4`. Thus the Euler equations
\[
 X_i+r_iX_i^s=\sum_z\eta_zq_{zi}+\Psi_i u_i
\]
hold exactly, along with every mass, base-moment, cover-contact, and complementarity equation from the normal stress theorem.

Nevertheless, for the positive cap the ratios are
\[
 (\delta_{-1},\delta_0,\delta_1)=(1/2,1,1/2),\qquad
 E_\pi\delta=2/3,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}_\pi(\delta)=1/18.
\]
Their covariance with Z is zero, so this entire variance is the undetected residual in (5). Equation (3) is an equality:
\[
 \Psi_+=\frac12\left(\frac43+\frac16\right)=\frac34.
\]
Dropping the variance would incorrectly give `Psi_+<=2/3`.

The body is centrally symmetric, so its origin has actual depth one half and the two displayed opposite caps are active depth caps. Thus the example also retains an actual maximizing mixed center and its full section-centroid equations. It refutes elimination of the slope variance from those normal/centroid identities. It does not refute any implication whose essential additional hypothesis is a cap budget below OC.
